old_title: Andy Burnham latest: Labour make spending promise after Trump's Falklands threat
new_title: Burnham blames Brexit for decade of UK decline
old_text:
John Healey has promised to hike UK defence spending after Donald Trump said he was reviewing the United States' position on the British sovereignty over the Falkland islands.
The US president is reportedly willing to British rule of the overseas territory as an incentive to encourage Andy Burnham to increase defence spending.
"I always review every position," Mr Trump told reporters on Monday, when asked about the islands' sovereignty. "That's just one of many," he added.
Speaking to The Times shortly after, Mr Healey insisted he was "100 per cent" committed to delivering a defence spending target of 3 per cent of GDP, adding he would set out the plan at the spring review.
It comes as Mr Burnham is set to deliver his first address as prime minister in the House of Commons on Tuesday as Parliament returns from recess this week.
The speech will focus on the cost-of-living crisis as the Labour leader makes a case for bringing more essential services under public control, according to reports in The Guardian.
Mr Burnham has announced a range of policies over the summer that have largely gone uncontested but will now face scrutiny by MPs.
Badenoch appoints architect of Truss's mini-Budget to replace Mel Stride as shadow chancellor
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has ruthlessly sacked her shadow chancellor, Sir Mel Stride, and replaced him with one of the architects of Liz Truss's disastrous mini-Budget.
New shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith was financial secretary to the Treasury - number three in the department - when Ms Truss's mini-Budget caused a run on the gilt market and almost bankrupted the country.
Ms Truss led the congratulations of Mr Griffith on his appointment, tweeting: "Congratulations to Andrew Griffith on becoming Shadow Chancellor. The economic establishment of the last three decades has failed Britain. They must be taken on."
Mr Griffith was a strong advocate of the former prime minister's plans to slash taxes and his appointment appears to be an indication that Ms Badenoch wants the party to take a more aggressive direction after the cautious approach of Sir Mel.

UK looks to 'refresh' US special relationship as Trump reignites Falklands row
John Healey has suggested he wants to "refresh" the special relationship with the United States, just hours after Donald Trump reignited a row over the Falklands Islands.
The US president suggested he was reconsidering US support for Britain's sovereignty over the Falkland Islands - remarks which are likely to inflame tensions with the UK even further. The islands are administered by the UK but are claimed by Argentina, whose president, Javier Millei, is an ally of Mr Trump.
But speaking to The Times, the chancellor insisted that, "just like in defence, the US is the UK's most important economic partner".

Trump says he is reviewing US position on Falkland Islands
President Donald Trump said he was reviewing the United States' position on the British sovereignty over the Falkland islands, in a move that will raise alarm for Labour ministers.
It follows reports last week that the US administration was prepared to oppose British rule of the overseas territory as an incentive to encourage Andy Burnham to increase defence spending,
The islands are administered by the UK but are claimed by Argentina, whose president is an ally of Mr Trump.
"I always review every position," Mr Trump told reporters on Monday, when asked about the islands' sovereignty. "That's just one of many," he added.

Prisons will still be able to function properly under new plans, minister insists
The justice secretary has insisted prisons will "still function properly" amid concerns over government plans to turn laundries into accommodation in a bid to tackle overcrowding.
Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Alex Norris told BBC Breakfast: "Of course we're going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.
"This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise."
He said ministers "want to improve the prison environment".
Live: Burnham to face off with Badenoch as he enters Commons as PM for first time
'Burnham bounce' is over, pollsters warn
The "Burnham bounce" has ended, just weeks after the new prime minister entered Downing Street, leading pollsters have said, as they warned there would be no point in Labour calling an early election.
Labour surged in the polls by around five to six points - finally leapfrogging Nigel Farage's Reform UK after 18 months - after Andy Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer on 20 July.
But experts say any bounce triggered by the change of leadership appears to have already peaked, with Labour failing to make any gains since last week - and even falling behind Reform again in some cases.
The Independent's political editor David Maddox has this exclusive report:
Davey says Labour's prison plans 'do not go far enough'
Plans by ministers to tackle overcrowding in prisons do not go far enough, the leader of the Liberal Democrats has suggested.
Sir Ed Davey told LBC Radio: "They're talking about turning laundries into prison cells in existing prisons.
"I'm not sure if that cuts it, to be honest ... and there's no new money.
"If they're going to get serious, they've really got to tackle it with a little bit more vigour and verve than I've seen so far. It's really, really important."
Victims whose perpetrators eligible for early release 'will be asked what restrictions they want imposed'
Victims whose perpetrators are due for early prison release will be asked what restrictions they want imposed "so they can live their life fully", the justice secretary has said.
Alex Norris told BBC Breakfast: "They will be written to. Letters start going out today.
"They will all be contacted individually by a victim liaison officer, who will then talk to them about, firstly, is their perpetrator coming out sooner than they expected? But secondly - and this is really crucial - that if their perpetrator is coming out sooner, or indeed when their perpetrator comes out in the future, what sort of controls do they want to see so they can live their life fully?"
He said offenders would be "subject to the widest range of tools we've ever had", including restriction zones, tagging, bans on attending football games or night clubs.
Mr Norris continued: "We will be talking through our victim liaison officers to victims and survivors to ask them how they live their lives, so that we can design the restrictions on their perpetrator, so that they live around their victims and survivors, rather than the other way round, which has been the case for far too long."
He encouraged victims to join the victim contact scheme.
Labour's prisons plan will create 'hundreds' of new places, justice secretary says
Justice secretary Alex Norris has declined to say whether there are fewer prison places than a year ago and insisted Labour's plans will create "hundreds" of new places.
Speaking to Times Radio on Tuesday morning ahead of setting out the plans to tackle overcrowding in the prisons estate in Parliament, he was asked about the Conservatives' claim that there are 700 fewer prison places than in 2025.
Mr Norris said: "Those wouldn't necessarily be the numbers I'd use, but it is possible that places come out of the estate. For example, you know, there can be damage, fire damage. We've got a very old estate.
"I talk about the biggest prison-building programme since the Victorian era. Well, that means that a lot of our estate is Victorian estate."
The estate "fluctuates" because of planned and unplanned conditions, the minister added.
Mr Norris said the plan to convert unused spaces inside prisons, such as shared use areas and offices, into new cells would create "in the hundreds of places".
"In a system that's running very hot, a few hundred places here and there makes a really big difference," he said.
Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle shows Conservatives 'have learned nothing', Labour chairwoman says
Bridget Philipson, Labour Party chairwoman, said Kemi Badenoch's shake-up of her shadow cabinet shows the Conservatives "have learnt nothing since they were kicked out of office by the British people".
She said in a statement: "Promoting a key architect of Liz Truss's disastrous mini Budget tells you all you need to know about Badenoch's complete lack of judgement.
"The Tories' top team is crammed full of the same vandals who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling. No wonder they've made no progress in the last two years.
"Meanwhile, Andy Burnham's Labour Government is driving good growth in every postcode, giving vital breathing space on the cost of living, and bringing back hope to Britain."
new_text:
Andy Burnham has lashed out at the legacy of Brexit, saying it "ushered in a decade of low growth" which the UK is still paying for, as he made his first statement as prime minister to the Commons.
In an unexpected attack on the legacy of leaving the EU, he listed the "series of wrong turns" the UK has made since the 1980s and warned Brexit had embedded the problems caused by over-centralisation of government, deindustrialisation and privatisation of industry.
The statement was framed as Mr Burnham laying out his vision for government after he took over from Sir Keir Starmer in a bloodless coup in July. But while he has stated he will stick to Sir Keir's red lines on Brexit of not rejoining the EU, single market or customs union, his words will provide hope that he may well look to change course by the next election.
In his statement, Mr Burnham also laid out his other key priorities:
- He paid tribute to Sir Keir Starmer, who announced he was quitting as an MP after being ousted from Downing Street
- He recommitted the UK's support for Ukraine and praised his Tory and Labour predecessors in providing the leadership to take on Vladimir Putin
- Insisted he would not back down from net zero policies in the wake of the climate crisis being responsible for the major flash flooding tragedy in Nepal
- But he ducked questions from Tory leader Kemi Badenoch on defence spending, taxes and cutting the welfare bill
- And he hinted electoral reform could be on the cards after Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey called for a national commission to change politics
The statement marked a significant change of tone from Sir Keir's two years in office, with Mr Burnham emphasising that he wanted to move away from "point scoring" to working with other parties to fix problems.
He warned: "Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should. Life is too expensive and too hard for too many. This is why this government's first moves were to give businesses and people a little breathing space."
Turning to the series of wrong turns that have led to the decline of living standards in the UK, he made a point of blasting Brexit, having said a year ago when he was mayor of Manchester that he favoured rejoining the EU.
He told MPs: "From the 1980s, this country took a series of wrong turns. Political power was centralised, economic power privatised. The country deindustrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this, and then Brexit, compounding the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration."
The comments have been welcomed by pro-EU campaigners just days after The Independent revealed the £11.7bn a year loss in exports Brexit has caused for British business as well as a survey showing 98.2 per cent of businesses want the UK to rejoin the single market.
Already, Mr Burnham is taking action on decentralisation with a new devolution agenda to hand powers to elected mayors, and he also vowed to take things back into public ownership, hinting that water companies could be an early target.
Pro-EU campaigners now hope he will apply the same logic to reversing Brexit.
Naomi Smith, chief executive of Best for Britain, said: "It's hugely welcome to hear a prime minister stand at the despatch box and say loudly and clearly that Brexit harmed Britain; far from taking back control, it shrank our economy, left us poorer, weaker, less safe and more divided."
She warned: "If Burnham is serious about delivering a politics done differently - and giving the public what our polling proves they want more of - he must keep all options on the table to single-mindedly pursue the profound economic transformation - some £92bn at the very least - that rejoining the EU would mean for our economy, while persuading progressives who have abandoned the party to trust Labour with their votes.
"That's how you get good growth in every postcode, and how you deliver hope in every heart."
But his claims were mocked by Ms Badenoch, who chided the new prime minister for not being available to be scrutinised by MPs for his first 43 days in office.
With Labour MPs chuntering in the background, she said: "The year is 2026. Yet the prime minister said in his statement that everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher.
"I may not look it, but I'm 46 years old. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past, and he wants to take us back to the 1970s. On this side of the house, we [Conservatives] are for the future not the past."
The intervention by Mr Burnham identifying Brexit as a "wrong turn" will raise hopes that his pledge last week to stick to Sir Keir's red lines can be reversed by the time of the next election.
Former prime minister Sir John Major warned in an interview with The Independent that the first priority of any prime minister must be to get the UK back into the EU's single market as a precursor to fully rejoining the bloc to reverse the economic decline caused by leaving the EU.
Mike Galsworthy, chair of the European Movement UK, told The Independent: "The biggest opportunity for Andy Burnham lies less in how he handles Starmer's restrictions from the last Labour manifesto and much more in the bigger move he can make with the next manifesto. A promise in the next manifesto to open accession talks for full EU membership is the prize here."
